title: Government health experts on air pollution: causes, who suffers and what should happen next
label: 14 September 2026 · Air Pollution in England
summary: Ministers and the Chief Medical Officer told MPs that air pollution causes large burdens of illness and hundreds of deaths each week, that the health department’s role is to make the medical case across Government, and that progress has been made but more coordinated action, better monitoring, clearer clinical advice and targeted local measures are needed to protect the most vulnerable.

chapters.title: Who’s here and who’s responsible
chapters.takeaway: The health department supplies the medical evidence and wants other departments to act—air pollution is a cross‑government issue.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Welcome. We wanted the housing ministry too because planning and construction matter for pollution, but they didn't send anyone. Today we have the Public Health Minister, the Chief Medical Officer and a DHSC official.

turns.speaker: Dame Diana Johnson
turns.text: I'm Diana Johnson, the new Public Health and Patient Safety Minister. My job is to bring the health case to other Departments so they factor in the health harms of dirty air.

turns.speaker: Professor Sir Chris Whitty
turns.text: I'm Chris Whitty, Chief Medical Officer. I lead on public health advice across Government and published a detailed report on air pollution in 2022.

turns.speaker: Simon Reeve
turns.text: I'm Simon Reeve, deputy director for public health systems at DHSC. My team handles air pollution policy in the Department.

chapters.title: How air pollution affects health and where it comes from
chapters.takeaway: Air pollution harms people across their lives—premature birth, asthma, heart disease, dementia—and main sources include transport, farming, construction and some home heating.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Can you summarise the main health impacts and what makes the worst pollution?

turns.speaker: Professor Sir Chris Whitty
turns.text: Air pollution is a major cause of illness and early death. A respected estimate is about 30,000 deaths a year in the UK; that’s a central estimate, not a precise count.

turns.speaker: Professor Sir Chris Whitty
turns.text: It affects people from before birth—premature birth and poor lung growth—to childhood asthma, and in adults drives heart disease, strokes, some cancers, dementia and long lung disease.

turns.speaker: Professor Sir Chris Whitty
turns.text: Key sources: transport (cars, trucks), construction dust, farming emissions—particularly ammonia from fertiliser and livestock—space heating (solid fuel and old stoves), and indoor sources.

turns.speaker: Professor Sir Chris Whitty
turns.text: Pollution particles called PM2.5 are important; some pollutants travel across borders so international standards matter too.

turns.speaker: Dame Diana Johnson
turns.text: DHSC’s role is to supply the scientific evidence to DEFRA—the environment department—and other Departments so they make policies that protect health.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: You say there’s been progress; is the position getting better?

turns.speaker: Professor Sir Chris Whitty
turns.text: Yes. The previous estimate was higher—about 40,000 a decade ago—so regulations and technology have helped. But big gains remain possible.

chapters.title: Targets, monitoring and who bears the burden
chapters.takeaway: UK legal limits lag the World Health Organization’s tighter guidelines, monitoring is patchy in places, and deprived communities suffer most.

turns.speaker: Jonathan Davies
turns.text: If UK legal limits allow levels that still cause harm, why keep them? Should we move toward WHO guidelines?

turns.speaker: Professor Sir Chris Whitty
turns.text: From a health view, we should reduce pollution as far as practical. WHO tightened its guidance in 2021; targets are political decisions but we should keep pushing downward.

turns.speaker: Martin Rhodes
turns.text: How are health inequalities being tackled—kids, deprived areas, ethnic minorities are worst affected—who measures that?

turns.speaker: Dame Diana Johnson
turns.text: Reducing the gap in healthy life expectancy is in our 10-year plan. Public Health England (now UKHSA) has an air quality and health dashboard for local authorities to see pollution and local demographics.

turns.speaker: Professor Sir Chris Whitty
turns.text: People in poorer areas get a double hit: worse baseline health and higher pollution. That’s why cutting pollution for everyone helps the most, but we also need targeted local action.

turns.speaker: Sojan Joseph
turns.text: Clinicians don't always mention air quality to patients—are they given clear guidance, especially for vulnerable people?

turns.speaker: Professor Sir Chris Whitty
turns.text: Most clinicians know air pollution is a risk, but it's harder to tell an individual what to do. There's guidance and tools—like air-quality indices on apps—and professional bodies have started to include air quality in training.

turns.speaker: Professor Sir Chris Whitty
turns.text: Monitoring is useful but not perfect. We need denser monitoring in urban areas and around schools, hospitals and care homes where vulnerable people concentrate.

turns.speaker: Barry Gardiner
turns.text: Why hasn’t the UK updated legal limits to match the EU or WHO, so one part of the UK or Europe isn’t better protected?

turns.speaker: Dame Diana Johnson
turns.text: DEFRA sets targets and is reviewing the air quality strategy. As Public Health Minister I’ll make the medical case, but target changes are for DEFRA Ministers.

chapters.title: What actions help most and who should do them
chapters.takeaway: Big wins come from coordinated national, local and international action—cleaner vehicles, farming changes, tackling indoor pollution in public buildings—and better public and clinical communication.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Which government actions would make the biggest difference quickly?

turns.speaker: Professor Sir Chris Whitty
turns.text: International vehicle standards have driven big falls in road emissions. Electrifying fleets, reducing agricultural ammonia (which forms particles), stopping pointless diesel idling and swapping very polluting home heating all help.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: What about indoor pollution and public messages—should there be a national campaign?

turns.speaker: Professor Sir Chris Whitty
turns.text: Indoor pollution is becoming more important as outdoor levels fall. Public buildings—hospitals, libraries, supermarkets—are like outdoors because people have to use them; we should prioritise those environments.

turns.speaker: Dame Diana Johnson
turns.text: We already have tools: the daily air-quality index, DEFRA alerts people can sign up to, and an Air Pollution Awareness Coalition—DEFRA convenes academics, health professionals and charities to coordinate messaging.

turns.speaker: Adrian Ramsay
turns.text: How far have we come on training doctors so advising patients about pollution is routine?

turns.speaker: Professor Sir Chris Whitty
turns.text: We're maybe halfway there. Air quality should be in medical school curricula and more in postgraduate training. Royal colleges have done some work, but it needs to be wider and more practical.

turns.speaker: Dame Diana Johnson
turns.text: Other health professionals matter too—health visitors and nurses can help families with practical advice, not just doctors.

turns.speaker: Jonathan Davies
turns.text: Do Treasury, the Cabinet Office and business departments grasp the health case—some local clean-air plans meet resistance?

turns.speaker: Dame Diana Johnson
turns.text: Air pollution must be cross‑government. Local decisions differ—mayors can invest in electric buses instead of zone charges—but the outcome we all want is lower pollution.

chapters.title: Planning, law and next steps
chapters.takeaway: Legal changes, local planning inputs from public health, and learning from international farming and transport practice are on the table, but legal choices are for politicians to decide.

turns.speaker: Manuela Perteghella
turns.text: Should public health be a formal consultee on planning? Houses have been built next to busy roads without pollution considered.

turns.speaker: Dame Diana Johnson
turns.text: Local public health directors do good work and have a role. I’ll look at whether making that a formal duty would help—local planning should consider health impacts.

turns.speaker: Professor Sir Chris Whitty
turns.text: From a professional view, I want public health input on planning. Making it statutory is a political decision, but informed local decisions benefit from that expertise.

turns.speaker: Adrian Ramsay
turns.text: What about Ella’s law—the proposed Clean Air (Human Rights) Bill that would make clean air a legal right?

turns.speaker: Professor Sir Chris Whitty
turns.text: Ella’s tragic death has rightly pushed action. The principle of stronger protections is right, but deciding whether a Bill is the right route is for elected politicians, not me.

turns.speaker: Professor Sir Chris Whitty
turns.text: Internationally we can learn a lot—some countries cut agricultural ammonia a lot, and others have moved faster on electrifying high‑risk urban transport.

turns.speaker: Barry Gardiner
turns.text: The death toll from air pollution is far larger than many other causes we debate—are we politically doing enough?

turns.speaker: Professor Sir Chris Whitty
turns.text: We have made progress and saved lives, but more gains are possible and would reduce disease. Policy, law and engineering choices drive these further improvements.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Thank you all. We'll publish this evidence and continue to press for joined‑up action, better monitoring and clearer clinical and public messaging.

glossary.definition: The UK Department of Health and Social Care, the government department responsible for national health policy and NHS oversight.
Fine particulate matter with diameter 2.5 micrometres or less that can penetrate lungs and bloodstream and harm health.
The World Health Organization, the United Nations agency that issues international public‑health guidance and standards.
UK Health Security Agency, the national agency (successor to Public Health England) that protects the public from health threats and hazards.
A DEFRA‑convened group of academics, health professionals and charities that coordinate public messaging on air pollution.
A daily numeric or colour-coded scale that shows local pollution levels and gives simple health advice for the public.
A popular name for a proposed campaign law, inspired by a child named Ella, aiming to make clean air a legal right.
A proposed UK bill to recognise clean air as a legal right and require government action to protect air quality.
UK professional medical bodies (e.g. Royal College of Physicians) that set standards, training and exams for doctors.
The UK government department that coordinates policy across departments and supports the Prime Minister and Cabinet.
HM Treasury, the UK government department responsible for public spending, taxation and overall economic policy.
Local fees levied on vehicles entering designated urban zones to reduce traffic and improve air quality.
A legal term meaning required, created or enforceable by law.
Ammonia emissions from fertiliser and livestock that react in air to form fine particles harmful to health.
Local councils in the UK that deliver services like planning, public health, education and local regulation.
